entries.title: Mother who beat addiction fatally shot snuggling in bed with her 2 daughters, sister and police say
entries.summary: <p>Crystal Salter, inspired by the birth of her daughter, Juliana, spent the last several years of her life helping others climb out of the same drug-fueled position she once found herself in.</p><p>But her life ended abruptly and violently early Sunday.</p><p>That's when, police and relatives say, she was fatally shot by her boyfriend — in front of 7-year-old Juliana and Legacy, the 7-year-old foster daughter she took in this year. </p><p>A couple of hours later, Salter's boyfriend was found dead in his vehicle with a self-inflicted gunshot wound to his mouth, police said. </p><p>"It's unfortunate for her to lose her life to gun violence, for her to lose her life to a person she loved and adored so much," Regina Salter, Crystal Salter's younger sister, said. "It's sad we lost her like this." </p><p>Crystal Salter, 42, was in bed with the two children at her home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard when she was shot multiple times in her torso and face, police said. She was taken to Stroger Hospital where she was pronounced dead, officials said.</p><p>Juliana, now under her aunt's care, has struggled since her mother's slaying.</p><p>"Can I see my mommy? I want to see my mommy. I want to go home," Juliana will plead, Regina Salter said.</p><p>"I just have to go in one room and cry, or go out on the back porch and cry because there's no love like a mother's love," Regina Salter said. "You can't fill the void of a child's mother."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b10000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crystal Salter “always felt that God gave her a second chance” and that’s all she would talk about, her sister said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>‘He had a mask on his face’ </h3><p>Crystal Salter met her boyfriend at a South Side gas station last December, and he "worshipped the ground she walked on," Regina Salter said. </p><p>Issues in the relationship, potentially including Crystal Salter taking in Legacy after her mother checked out of a women's treatment center and disappeared, led Salter to give her boyfriend until the end of August to move out of her apartment, according to her sister. </p><p>But Regina Salter never got any inclination that the 49-year-old man, who hasn’t yet been identified by the Cook County medical examiner's office, was capable of such violence. </p><p>"He didn't come off as a person who would fight women or potentially would kill a woman," Regina Salter said. "We were all shocked." </p><p>Five shell casings were found in the bathroom of the apartment, and a large pool of blood was found on a bed, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. </p><p>In the vehicle where the man was found, officers discovered a Smith & Wesson revolver with four live rounds and a fired shell casing and four additional shell casings on the floorboard of the front passenger area. </p><p>"The first sign that you see from a man, it's time to leave, don't be afraid to reach out to some family or someone close and tell them what's going on," Regina Salter said. "The man that took my sister's life, he wore masks. He had a mask on his face. We didn't know he was like that."</p><h3>Overcoming addiction to help others in a similar situation </h3><p>Crystal Salter was molested and raped in her early 20s, and the trauma led her to become heavily addicted to drugs for roughly a decade, according to her sister. Relatives didn’t know whether they'd lose her to her addiction. </p><p>"We would go see her and go drop her off food and go try and give her money and try to help her get better and get clean, but she didn't," Regina Salter said. "She just wouldn't get help."</p><p>But when she became pregnant with Juliana, Crystal Salter became inspired to get herself off drugs and start a new path forward. </p><p>"It changed Crystal's life for the better, and she got help. She recovered fast, and it made her want to be a voice for others," Regina Salter said. "That's what she's been doing for the last eight years of her life."</p><p>During one trip to Aldi, Crystal Salter saw a woman at a bus stop without shoes and demanded her sister pull over so she could give the woman the shoes off her feet, family recalls. She walked around in socks until she bought a pair of shoes at Aldi. </p><p>"She always felt that God gave her a second chance by giving her Juliana, and that's all she would talk about," Regina Salter said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crystal (left) and Regina Salter had a strong sisterhood. Regina recalls Crystal helping her tie her shoes when they were young, and the sisters — the two youngest of 10 children — grew closer as they got older. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><p>Crystal Salter was never shy about sharing the more turbulent parts of her life with other in hopes of being an inspiration to those in similar circumstances.</p><p>Regina Salter used to advise against her sister sharing certain details about her life, but Crystal Salter stressed it was "her story to tell" and she wanted others to see "there are rainbows after the rain and you can get help and recover."</p><p>Crystal Salter was called a spiritual "beam of joy" involved with her church who also loved barbecue and had dreams of opening a women's shelter to help women and children in need. </p><p>Even after losing her mother to heart failure — her mom never knew she got clean — Crystal Salter stayed devoted to her improved lifestyle. </p><p>"She always was out there helping the community," Regina Salter said. "We were all just so proud of Crystal."</p><h3>Making ends meet to provide stability for a child in need </h3><p>In April, Crystal Salter was driving on the West Side when she spotted a woman she was once in a treatment center with sitting in an alley with her child. </p><p>She offered the woman and 7-year-old girl, Legacy, a place in her apartment before the woman checked herself into a treatment center and left hours later, Regina Salter said. </p><p>After failed attempts to reach Legacy's mother, Crystal Salter gained custody of Legacy days later and used money she saved and the income from work as a call center operator for SCR Transportation, a company that subcontracts to Pace, to provide schooling and stability for Legacy. </p><p>"That kind of position requires patience and kindness while working with vulnerable communities," according to Pace spokesperson Maggie Daly Skogsbakken. </p><p>Said Kristin Persu, a co-worker of Crystal Salter at SCR Transportation: “Crystal was a wonderful team member, and we are deeply saddened to learn of her passing. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family and friends during this difficult time.”</p><p>"She just loved being a mother," Regina Salter said. "So I'm thinking she seen Legacy needed some love, she needed to be in a stable household, she needed to probably get in school because Legacy had been living out on the streets with her mom."</p><div Crystal Salter saw the opportunity as a blessing. </p><p>"God has really answered my prayers," she posted on Facebook around the time she took Legacy in. "I am truly honored to have two little amazing girls in my life."</p><p>Since the fatal shooting, Juliana has been in the care of her aunt, while Legacy is with the parents of her uncle in Gurnee. </p><p>That uncle, Mark Weir, says Legacy and Juliana have not yet been in direct contact since Crystal Salter was killed, but he hopes to arrange a meeting soon.</p><p>Regina Salter hopes the two girls can continue to be in each other's lives. The two have talked over FaceTime and may see each other again in person at Crystal Salter's funeral next week. </p><p>"She wants to see her sister," Regina said of her niece. entries.title: Cubs have no animosity toward Brewers, even with another 2nd-place finish looming
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — Hot take: The White Sox-Brewers rivalry in the early days of the American League Central was much hotter than the Cubs-Brewers rivalry of today.</p><p>And those Sox-Brewers games in the mid-1990s never meant anything close to what Cubs-Brewers games have meant for the last decade. The Sox and Brewers never battled each other for first place or even a playoff spot.</p><p>But Sox manager Terry Bevington and Brewers manager Phil Garner, aka “Scrap Iron,” seemed to detest each other. Their feelings boiled over in 1995 when they wrestled in the middle of a benches-clearing brawl that ignited when Sox legend Ozzie Guillen got tangled with Jeff Cirillo after sliding into third base.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Brewers haven’t even given each other a side-eyed look, despite playing so many hotly contested games in the regular season and postseason.</p><p>Where’s the fun in that?</p><p>“It’s interesting that there can be both intensity, but not like it turns into other stuff too much,” Cubs infielder Nico Hoerner told the Sun-Times. “Both teams play the game pretty hard, but I don’t feel like either team is dirty.”</p><p>The Cubs are going to finish second to the Brewers in the National League Central for the fourth consecutive year and the third straight under manager Craig Counsell, whom they poached from the Brewers to beat them. Doesn’t that irritate anyone in the Cubs’ clubhouse?</p><p>“I know a lot of the guys on that team,” Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson told us. “It’s hard to have animosity toward good people.”</p><p>Maybe that’s why. There’s no one on either team who gets under the skin of the other team.</p><p>“There hasn’t been a moment of pettiness or bad blood,” Hoerner said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OyuoZW2pS6w?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Coaches get into a fight near third base"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>There could have been Monday. Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong led off the game with a bouncer to first baseman Andrew Vaughn, who bobbled the ball, stepped on the bag and got bowled over by Crow-Armstrong, who had nowhere to go.</p><p>But instead of igniting an all-out melee, Crow-Armstrong tried to soften Vaughn’s fall, put his arm around him and made sure he was OK.</p><p>What are these, the Friendship Games?</p><p>“There was no extra shove or anything like that,” Cubs pitcher Colin Rea, who has been on both sides of the rivalry — or whatever this is — told us. “It was an accident. If that was 20 years ago, he would have tried to take him out. But it’s just not the way the game is played right now.”</p><p>“Vaughn’s a great dude,” Swanson said. “I signed a bat for something he’s doing at his house.”</p><p>Maybe it stems from the managers, who have a decadeslong relationship. Brewers manager Pat Murphy was Cubs manager Craig Counsell’s coach at Notre Dame. When Counsell managed the Brewers, Murphy was his bench coach — for all nine seasons.</p><p>“They have a long history with each other. They have a good relationship,” Rea said. “Yeah, I think it could stem from that. If they didn’t get along, maybe that would trickle down to the players.”</p><p>Like it did for the Bears and Packers under former coaches Mike Ditka and Forrest Gregg, respectively, in the 1980s. Their relationship — or whatever it was — more closely resembled Bevington-Garner, without the fisticuffs. Though they did get into a shouting match — during a preseason game.</p><p>This is all to say that, while the Cubs and Brewers compete to the hilt against each other, they don’t dislike each other. At all.</p><p>Pity.</p><p>“There’s definitely competitiveness, talk amongst the team as far as how badly we want to win,” Rea said. “Being around that side, all those guys are great guys, and I see the same thing in this clubhouse. We have two very similar teams, so it’s hard to dislike guys on that team.”</p><p>“It’s not like animosity towards them as much as it is a great challenge for us to rise to the occasion,” Swanson said.<br></p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Sean Burke shelled as White Sox need quick answers for their flagging starting rotation
entries.summary: <p>Beginning with 7⅓ innings of one-run ball on June 18, Sean Burke put together a seven-outing run of a 1.42 ERA over 50⅔ innings, establishing the right-hander as the stabilizing force in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> starting rotation that sorely needed one.</p><p>On Tuesday night, with the Sox guarding a slim lead in the AL Central, the first seven Pirates hitters Burke faced all reached base. The first five balls put in play off the 26-year-old all sizzled off the bat at 99.5 mph or harder, and the score was lopsided before the clock hit 7 p.m.</p><p>After issuing eight walks in his outing before last, which he called “the worst athletic performance of my life,” Burke yielded a career-high seven runs on eight hits in a career-low 1⅓ innings against the Pirates, departing after walking the bases loaded in the second to a mix of jeers and supportive applause befitting a breakout star whose brilliance has helped make White Sox games in September relevant, and whose suddenly erratic performance made it distressing.</p><p>Despite the carnage, Burke’s 3.58 ERA and 156 innings both still pace the Sox rotation. That’s in spite of him not recording a quality start in his last five outings, though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/01/white-sox-prospect-tanner-mcdougal-looking-to-show-improved-mechanics-after-rocky-debut-colson-montgomery-davis-martin-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his 5⅔ scoreless innings in Houston last week</u></a> came as close as possible.</p><p>But that reflects the shaky state of a White Sox rotation already at the bottom of the league in total innings. Davis Martin made a strong return from the injured list last week, but Anthony Kay has failed to complete five innings in his last three outings, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/03/white-sox-keeping-luis-castillo-in-rotation-and-munetaka-murakami-high-in-batting-order-amid-struggles-will-venable-astros-road-trip-zach-bove-al-central-division-playoffs" target="_blank" ><u>Luis Castillo has a 7.25 ERA since being acquired last month</u></a>, and manager Will Venable used a bullpen game to seize a rubber match victory from the Twins on Sunday.</p><p>With the way Sox starters are stumbling near the season’s finish line, Venable could go that route again soon.</p><p>“That's a good indication of what it could look like,” said Venable, who indicated his pitcher usage might have the all-hands-on-deck flavor of a playoff series down the stretch. “We've got some pretty special arms [in the bullpen] that can obviously get swing and miss, get some outs. But they can do it over multiple innings."</p><p>Burke has rejected the notion that fatigue is a factor in his recent mechanical inconsistency, even with his prior professional career-high in innings in the rearview mirror. Sox pitching coaches indicated that Burke’s emergence this year has been helped by dropping his arm slot, reducing the frequency with which his breaking balls pop up out of his hand on release and reveal themselves to opposing hitters.</p><p>To even further simplify the cue to something that lines up with his best command, Burke informs that when his shoulders remain level with each other throughout his delivery, his pitches are more consistent. When it’s awry, as it has been recently, he can spiral.</p><p>“Getting a little bit out of slot, I have a bad habit when you can’t command the ball well, of <i>trying</i> to get the ball there,” Burke told the Sun-Times last week. “That just makes it worse, because you’re diving your body forward and your arm can be later again.”</p><p>Last week in Houston, Burke made the correction quickly enough to salvage a great outing. On Tuesday, things spiraled for Burke too quickly for any mid-game adjustment, and far too swiftly for a Sox offense that didn’t manage a baserunner off Pirates starter Bubba Chandler until the fifth inning.</p><p>With the Cleveland Guardians on their heels, the Sox need to restore a better version of Burke over the season’s final 2½ weeks, as he’s spent most of 2026 looking like the closest thing they have to a rotation anchor.</p><p>“There's this extra gear that he's shown flashes of,” said pitching coach Zach Bove. “He can do that at a high level for many more years to come.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Former White Sox' first-round pick Jacob Gonzalez returns to Rate Field after being traded in July
entries.summary: <p>Infielder <b>Jacob Gonzalez</b> was a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> first-round pick in 2023 and leading the minors in homers when he was called up earlier this year, but still suspected he could be the odd man out.</p><p>“I was always nervous,” Gonzalez told the Sun-Times on Tuesday, before his first game at Rate Field since being traded to the Pirates in July. “What’s going to happen when [<b>Munetaka Murakami</b>] comes back?”</p><p>A drastically reworked swing under hitting director <b>Ryan Fuller</b>’s tutelage, a blistering .317/.419/.668 start in Triple-A, and Murakami’s Grade 2 hamstring strain, all worked to grant the 24-year-old Gonzalez a 30-game run with the White Sox. He was no Murakami, posting a .683 OPS while manning first base in his stead, but showed mettle in batting 8-for-18 (.444) with runners in scoring position; including a June 27 walk-off single against the Royals.</p><p>Still, the writing was on the wall when Murakami returned. Gonzalez was optioned to Charlotte as the corresponding move, and when he was pulled two innings into his first game back in the minors, he didn’t think it was for a return trip to Chicago.</p><p>“I didn't get told until the game ended what happened, so I was just sitting in the clubhouse waiting,” Gonzalez said. “I had enough time to figure out I was probably traded, but just sitting around and not knowing anything, that was the craziest part.”</p><p>Rather than infield depth, the Sox felt Gonzalez’s 2026 turnaround from looking like a failed prospect was best used to acquire more draft capital. They traded Gonzalez and lefty <b>Brandon Eisert</b> to Pittsburgh for relief prospect <b>Jaden Woods</b> and the 34th overall pick, which they used on Nazareth Academy shortstop <b>Landon Thome</b>.</p><p>Acquired to give the Pirates a shortstop while <b>Konnor Griffin</b> was out with an injury, Gonzalez hasn’t yet inspired regret. Entering Tuesday, Gonzalez has a .595 OPS with Pittsburgh, and is bouncing around the infield now that Griffin has returned. Gonzalez still stays in touch with his old teammates, and is even planning a December trip to Japan with <b>Sam Antonacci, Rikuu Nishida</b> and others, but betrayed no big emotions about returning to where it started.</p><p>“Feels like a normal road trip for me, but it’ll be fun to play against some of my friends,” said Gonzalez, who appreciates looking over his shoulder less at his new place. “It’s probably been better for me to come up here and struggle a bit, because that means I got to figure some new things out.”</p><h3><b>Brazoban at the ready</b></h3><p>Acquired at last month’s trade deadline to boost the bullpen, right-hander <b>Huascar Brazoban</b> is back in Chicago after two scoreless appearances in his Triple-A rehab assignment for a left lat strain. But the White Sox aren’t rushing him back into action.</p><p>“He's on the taxi squad right now,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b> “In case there's a need over the next couple of days, he'll be close by.”</p><p>Brazoban had yielded runs in five of his last six appearances prior to his injury.</p><h3><b>Dash in playoffs, sans Wolkow</b></h3><p>The Winston-Salem Dash, the Sox’ High-A affiliate, began a best-of-three series against Bowling Green in the South Atlantic League playoffs. They’re playing without 20-year-old Downers Grove-native <b>George Wolkow</b>, who posted a 22-homer, 100-RBI season, after he suffered a hairline fracture of his left big toe on a slide.</p>

entries.title: Ranking the 10 best senior basketball players in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>The prospect rankings in the Class of 2027 in Illinois are unlike any other year in state history.</p><p>Simply put, the college commitments and recruiting lists for players ranked in the top 10 in Illinois aren’t anywhere near the level we’ve ever seen. Just one example: It’s the Ivy League and mid-major conferences — not the Big Ten — battling for the state’s top talent.</p><p>But there will always be an asterisk attached to this class.</p><p>Keep in mind, there are five nationally ranked players who will all be headed to high-major programs who began their high school basketball careers in Illinois.</p><p>The names are familiar, including Davion Thompson (Bolingbrook), who actually has reclassified and is a freshman at Arkansas, Devin Cleveland (Kenwood), Jaxson Davis (Warren), Howard Williams (Young) and Illinois commit Quinton Kitt (East Peoria). They all left for prep schools.</p><p>As a result, here are the top 10 prospects as they begin their senior year.</p><h3>1. Ed Stasys, Benet</h3><p>Stasys has earned his unexpected rise to the top spot. After an impressive spring and summer full of production, the ultra-competitive 6-8 big man is set to show he’s more than just an elite defensive player and rebounder with toughness.</p><h3>2. Mason Martin, Neuqua Valley</h3><p>The best shooter in the class boasts size at 6-4 and a quick release to go with his unlimited range. Adding strength and evolving his game will come in time for the Illinois commit.</p><h3>3. J’dyn Lloyd, Belleville West</h3><h3></h3><p>A physically imposing player with athletic gifts, the 6-5 Lloyd certainly looks the part. But an improved jumper and consistency elevated his stock. He’s committed to Missouri State.</p><h3>4. Alex Sirbu, Buffalo Grove</h3><h3></h3><p>From the time this class entered high school, there might not be a more improved player than the 6-9 Sirbu. An elite rebounder with size and strength, Sirbu is headed to Columbia in the Ivy League over other mid-major opportunities.</p><h3>5. Jamier Montgomery, Crane</h3><h3></h3><p>What a spectacular few weeks the smooth combo scoring guard put together in June and July. He grabbed a lot of worthy attention and was an instant mid-major target, ultimately committing to Kent State.</p><h3>6. Hayden Schroeder, Wheaton Academy</h3><h3></h3><p>All the 6-7 Schroeder has done throughout his career is produce. And he does his offensive damage with his back to the basket and with an improving face-up jumper.</p><h3>7. Mikey Woods, Perspectives-Leadership</h3><p>He’s new to the city and to the rankings, returning to Chicago after playing his freshman year at St. Francis de Sales. But he’s a high-motor, aggressive and talented guard with Division I ability.</p><h3>8. Markese Peoples, St. Laurence</h3><h3></h3><p>A breakout junior year was followed by an impressive spring that warranted more attention. It’s so difficult to divert the physical, big-bodied guard from the basket. Headed to Central Michigan.</p><h3>9. Kendall Meyers, Marist</h3><h3></h3><p>A seasoned player who helped the RedHawks to a state title last season, look for the 6-5 jack-of-all-trades Meyers to blossom as a senior as his role and opportunity expands.</p><h3>10. Ryan Howard, Alton</h3><h3></h3><p>A versatile and underrated player in the southern part of the state who impacts the game in a variety of ways and affects winning. Howard is staying close to home and headed to SIUE.</p>
